candidates.quote: The quality of mercy is not strained. / It droppeth as the gentle rain from heaven / Upon the place beneath. It is twice blest: / It blesseth him that gives and him that takes.
candidates.author: William Shakespeare
candidates.locator: Act 4, scene 1, Portia to Shylock; Folger Shakespeare Library edition, 4.1.190 to 193 (the Folger web reader numbers them 2099 to 2102)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The most famous account of mercy in the language says it costs nothing, falls like weather, and does good twice: once to the one who gets it and once to the one who gives.
candidates.speaker: Portia

candidates.quote: ’Tis not my nature to join in hating, but in loving.
candidates.author: Sophocles
candidates.locator: line 523, Antigone to Creon; The Antigone of Sophocles, ed. and trans. R. C. Jebb (Cambridge University Press, 1891)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Asked to hate on command, Antigone answers with the one sentence the play is remembered by: her nature is to love, and she will not be argued out of it.
candidates.speaker: Antigone

candidates.quote: I am a man, and nothing that concerns a man do I deem a matter of indifference to me.
candidates.author: Terence
candidates.locator: Act 1, scene 1, line 77, Chremes to Menedemus; The Comedies of Terence, trans. Henry Thomas Riley (Harper and Brothers, 1874)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Homo sum: the Roman stage line that Augustine says the whole theatre applauded, because it refuses to let any other person’s trouble be none of your business.
candidates.speaker: Chremes

candidates.quote: You must sit down, sayes Love, and taste my meat: / So I did sit and eat.
candidates.author: George Herbert
candidates.locator: lines 17 and 18, the closing lines; The Temple: Sacred Poems and Private Ejaculations (Cambridge, 1633), the last poem of The Church
candidates.whyThisMonth: The last poem of The Temple ends with a guest who feels unworthy being told, kindly and firmly, to sit down and be fed: the plainest picture of welcome in English verse.

candidates.quote: On that best portion of a good man’s life; / His little, nameless, unremembered acts / Of kindness and of love.
candidates.author: William Wordsworth
candidates.work: Lines written a few miles above Tintern Abbey
candidates.locator: lines 34 to 36 of the 1798 printing (35 to 37 in the standard numbering); Lyrical Ballads (J. and A. Arch, 1798)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The best part of a good life, Wordsworth says, is made of small kindnesses nobody records and nobody remembers, which is a manageable ambition for one ordinary morning.

candidates.quote: If I can stop one heart from breaking, / I shall not live in vain; / If I can ease one life the aching, / Or cool one pain, / Or help one fainting robin / Unto his nest again, / I shall not live in vain.
candidates.author: Emily Dickinson
candidates.work: ‘If I can stop one heart from breaking’ (Franklin 982; Johnson 919)
candidates.locator: Poems by Emily Dickinson, ed. Mabel Loomis Todd and T. W. Higginson (Roberts Brothers, 1890), Life VI, the whole poem
candidates.whyThisMonth: Seven lines that set the bar for a worthwhile day at exactly one heart, one pain, one robin: kindness at a scale a person can actually reach before breakfast.

candidates.quote: For there is no friend like a sister / In calm or stormy weather; / To cheer one on the tedious way, / To fetch one if one goes astray, / To lift one if one totters down, / To strengthen whilst one stands.
candidates.author: Christina Rossetti
candidates.locator: lines 562 to 567, the closing lines, Laura to the children; Goblin Market and Other Poems (Macmillan, 1862)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The poem ends by turning its whole story into a lesson for children: what a friend is for, told as a list of things to do for someone on a hard road.
candidates.speaker: Laura

candidates.quote: He drew a circle that shut me out — / Heretic, rebel, a thing to flout. / But Love and I had the wit to win: / We drew a circle that took him in!
candidates.author: Edwin Markham
candidates.locator: the whole quatrain, p. 1 (Voluntaries); The Shoes of Happiness, and Other Poems (Doubleday, Page, 1915)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The month’s blurb in four lines: the answer to being shut out is not a smaller circle but a bigger one, drawn wide enough to include the person who drew the first.

candidates.quote: Here is thy footstool and there rest thy feet where live the poorest, and lowliest, and lost.
candidates.author: Rabindranath Tagore
candidates.locator: poem 10, opening sentence; Gitanjali (India Society, London, 1912; Macmillan, 1913), the author’s own English
candidates.whyThisMonth: Tagore locates the sacred not above the poorest and lowliest but among them, so that to widen the circle is simply to go where it already rests.
candidates.translator: Rabindranath Tagore, the author’s own English, 1912

candidates.quote: Don’t kill that fly! / Look—it’s wringing its hands, / wringing its feet.
candidates.author: Kobayashi Issa
candidates.work: ‘Don’t kill that fly’ (yare utsu na / hae ga te o suri / ashi o suru)
candidates.locator: The Essential Haiku: Versions of Bashō, Buson, and Issa, ed. and trans. Robert Hass (Ecco, 1994), Issa section
candidates.whyThisMonth: Issa’s most famous haiku extends mercy to the smallest thing in the room, by noticing that it, too, is pleading.
candidates.year: c. 1821 (composed; Hachiban nikki, the Eighth Diary)

candidates.quote: Little feet of children / blue with cold, / how can they see you and not cover you— / dear God!
candidates.author: Gabriela Mistral
candidates.locator: lines 1 to 4, the opening stanza; Selected Poems of Gabriela Mistral, trans. Doris Dana (Johns Hopkins, 1971); Spanish in Desolación (1922)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The poem every Chilean schoolchild learns opens with a plain question about compassion: how can anyone look at cold feet and not cover them?

candidates.quote: Warning, in music-words / devout and large, / that we are each other’s / harvest: / we are each other’s / business: / we are each other’s / magnitude and bond.
candidates.author: Gwendolyn Brooks
candidates.locator: lines 10 to 17, the closing lines; Family Pictures (Broadside Press, 1970)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Three short declarations that other people are not optional: we are each other’s harvest, business, and bond, which is the whole month in one closing sentence.

candidates.quote: My heart is moved by all I cannot save: / so much has been destroyed / I have to cast my lot with those / who age after age, perversely, / with no extraordinary power, / reconstitute the world.
candidates.author: Adrienne Rich
candidates.locator: the closing six lines; The Dream of a Common Language: Poems 1974 to 1977 (W. W. Norton, 1978)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Compassion that does not wait for extraordinary power: Rich casts her lot with the ordinary people who mend the world again every morning, and invites the reader to join them.

candidates.author: Elizabeth Bishop
candidates.locator: the closing line; Questions of Travel (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1965)
candidates.whyThisMonth: After six stanzas of grime and small tended details, the poem arrives at four words of unearned assurance: somebody is looking after all of us, even here.

candidates.quote: You do not have to be good. / You do not have to walk on your knees / for a hundred miles through the desert repenting. / You only have to let the soft animal of your body / love what it loves.
candidates.author: Mary Oliver
candidates.locator: lines 1 to 5, the opening; Dream Work (Atlantic Monthly Press, 1986), p. 14
candidates.whyThisMonth: The most quoted opening in late twentieth-century American poetry starts the day by lifting the demand to be good and replacing it with permission to be kind, first of all to yourself.

candidates.quote: Then it is only kindness that makes sense anymore, / only kindness that ties your shoes / and sends you out into the day to mail letters and purchase bread, / only kindness that raises its head / from the crowd of the world to say / It is I you have been looking for, / and then goes with you everywhere / like a shadow or a friend.
candidates.author: Naomi Shihab Nye
candidates.locator: the closing eight lines; Words Under the Words: Selected Poems (Far Corner Books, 1995); first in Different Ways to Pray (Breitenbush, 1980)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The poem the word kindness now belongs to ends with kindness doing the morning’s smallest jobs, tying shoes and sending you out for bread, and then keeping you company all day.
